names.name: Exam charm
names.said: gōkaku kigan, 'prayer for passing'; in Korean, the gift is yeot (엿) or chapssaltteok (찹쌀떡)
names.th: เครื่องรางสอบผ่าน (โกกากุ คิกัง)

etymology.root: Japanese 合格祈願 gōkaku kigan, from 合格 gōkaku 'passing an examination' and 祈願 kigan 'prayer, petition'
etymology.note: The commercial category is gōkaku kigan shōhin, goods for the prayer to pass. The Kit Kat leg of it runs on a different mechanism: きっと勝つとぉ kitto katsutoo, a Kyushu phrase meaning 'you shall surely win', which is what キットカット Kitto Katto sounds like.

text.what: Four different objects doing one job. A brocade pouch a few centimetres long, the shrine's name woven into it, a paper or wooden prayer sealed inside and not to be opened. A wooden plaque about 15 by 9 centimetres, written on and hung at the shrine. A two-finger chocolate bar in a printed wrapper. A stick of boiled-down grain taffy. The first two come from a shrine; the last two come from a supermarket, and a student carries any of them into the same room.
text.story:
Japan's examination charm has a god, and he was a real man. Sugawara no Michizane was a Heian-period scholar and poet who was exiled to Kyushu and died there; he is enshrined as Tenjin, god of scholarship and learning — and of natural disasters, which is a detail worth keeping. Dazaifu Tenmangū, the shrine built where he was exiled, states it plainly on its own English page: "As Tenjin is the deity of learning, amulets for academic success are one of the most popular items to take home from Dazaifu Tenmangu." Many of the amulets carry the plum flower, which the shrine says Michizane loved and which is its symbol. The shrine's own framing of the exchange is careful and worth quoting as printed: "At Shinto shrines you can receive an omamori, or amulet, to bring good luck, for a small donation." Received, for a donation. Not bought.

The omamori for this is gakugyō-jōju, education and passing examinations, one of a standard list that also runs to traffic safety, safe childbirth, a good marriage, business prosperity and family peace. The rule is the same as for every omamori: do not open it, and return the old one to the shrine it came from — traditionally to be burnt rather than binned, out of respect to the deity that carried you through the year.

The second Japanese object is the Kit Kat, and the wordplay has to be got right. キットカット, Kitto Katto, is what the brand is called in Japanese. Kitto means surely. Katsu means to win. The Kyushu phrase is きっと勝つとぉ, kitto katsutoo, 'you shall surely win', and that is the thing the brand name sounds like. Peter Davis, writing for Japan House at the University of Illinois, gives the figure: "In fact, one in three students in Japan will buy a Kit-Kat in anticipation of entrance examinations." The English Wikipedia article is more guarded and says the marketing "is believed to have benefited from the coincidental false cognate", and that market research shows the brand strongly correlated with good-luck charms among students ahead of exams. *Inference —* the two accounts differ on how much of this Nestlé made and how much of it Nestlé found, and this project does not have the internal documents to settle that. What is dated is the marketing: the 'Lucky Charm' campaign won the Asian Brand Marketing Effectiveness Award in 2005, and in 2009 Nestlé and Japan Post ran a campaign letting people write on the bars and post them from 20,000 post offices — which won the Media Grand Prix at Cannes Lions in 2010.

Korea works the same joke on a different verb. Families and friends give a student 엿, yeot — a taffy boiled down from steamed rice, glutinous rice, sorghum, corn or sweet potato — and 찹쌀떡, chapssaltteok, glutinous rice cake, before the Suneung university entrance examination. Both are sticky. The Korean verb for sticking to something is also the verb for passing an exam, so the gift says what it means without saying it. The English Wikipedia entry on yeot confirms students receive it before examinations and otherwise concentrates on the same word's career as an obscenity, which is the other thing a Korean reader knows about it.

The shrine end of the trade has been argued about in public, with a date attached. In 1979 two shrines dedicated to education sold ema — the wooden prayer plaques — for examination success; after public outcry, the funds were turned into a scholarship in 1980. *Inference —* that is the cleanest instance this atlas has of a charm trade answering a complaint by converting the takings into the thing the charm was asking for.
text.how: An omamori is received at the shrine office for a donation, carried on the person or tied to a bag, not opened, and returned to the same shrine at the New Year to be burnt. An ema is bought at the shrine, written on, and hung on the rack until it is ritually burnt at a ceremony — the burning treated as freeing the wish. A Kit Kat is bought at a convenience store, sometimes posted, and eaten. Yeot and chapssaltteok are given by family and friends and eaten. Nothing consecrates the last two, and nobody claims anything does.
text.today: Running every winter. Japanese entrance-examination season and the Korean Suneung both fall in the cold months, and the shelves change accordingly. As of 2026 the shrine goods, the exam-season chocolate packaging and the taffy all coexist, with the shrine goods carrying a deity's name and the other two carrying a pun. No dated price was read for any of them, and neither Dazaifu Tenmangū's page nor the sources on the Korean gifts print one.

dating.period: the modern examination system; the Tenjin cult behind it is Heian
dating.label: the dated record runs from 1979; the Tenjin cult behind it is Heian; carried now
dating.note: 1979 is the earliest DATED event this project read in the exam-charm trade: two education shrines selling ema for examination success, with the proceeds turned into a scholarship in 1980 after public outcry. It is not the start of the practice, which is older and undated in these sources. The Kit Kat leg is dated separately: an award in 2005, a Japan Post campaign in 2009, a Cannes award in 2010. Sugawara no Michizane, enshrined as Tenjin, is a Heian-period figure, and the sources read here give no year for him.

object.made_by: shrines and temples, which make the omamori and the ema and may have factories make them when demand outruns the shrine; and, for the chocolate and the taffy, food manufacturers with no religious claim at all
object.inscription: the shrine's name woven into the omamori; a wish written by hand on the ema; a printed message on exam-season chocolate wrappers
object.note: Form is entered as packet for the omamori, which is the object a reader is likeliest to be holding. The genre also covers a wooden plaque, a chocolate bar and a stick of taffy, and no single form key carries all four. single_use is true in the sense that an omamori is customarily replaced once a year and an ema is burnt; the food is eaten. The ema measurement, about 15 cm by 9 cm, is published in the cited ema article. No measurement was read for the omamori, so no length_mm is entered for the record as a whole.

confusable_with.tell: this record is the examination variety and its commercial hangers-on; a plain omamori from the same counter may be for the road, a birth or a marriage, and the Japanese written on it says which
